utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Sachdeva, I'd like to ask Ms. Isailovic whether the Defence intends to make a Rule 98 bis submission tomorrow -- sorry, on Thursday, on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes. The Defence wishes to file a 98 bis before the Chamber, but we had planned to do this on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, actually, it's to be an oral submission, which is a submission to be made orally, and I'm trying to find out whether, in fact, it is not something which could be accommodated tomorrow, if we were to start at 8.00 in the morning, because, as you know, the amendment that was made in 2004 was really designed to promote expeditiousness in the consideration of this motion. And if you are to make your motion in a relatively short time and the Prosecution reply in a relatively short time, without doing any prejudice, of course, to the substance to the argument which you wish to present, then it is occurring to me, in fact, that we might be able to accommodate it tomorrow if we were to start at 8.00. So I would want to hear from you on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The idea then is that if we could do everything in an hour, hour and 20 minutes, we would then not need to meet on Thursday, but I would need to hear from you whether you think the submissions, which you have to make, could be made in a relatively short period of time if we were to start at 8.00 tomorrow morning, and then we would set aside, an hour, hour and 15 minutes for the submissions and the consideration of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm alone today, and I shall confer with Mr. Tapuskovic. I think it is most likely that this is something which we should be able to do tomorrow. But, if possible, because we haven't yet finished with this witness, I do hope that we will be able to finish with the expert today, and tomorrow we will have the last witness of the Prosecution. If we decided to start at 8.00, perhaps we could then, during the second session, once we have finished with the witness, we could then have a break and resume with our 98 bis motion, if this is amenable to you. I shall confer with Mr. Tapuskovic over the break, but this seems quite acceptable to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, of course, the length of our submission depends a little bit on what specifically is challenged by the Defence in its 98 bis submission. If the Defence challenges all of the counts, all of the elements, I anticipate that it would take us a full hour and a half to respond to that, to cover that, and make a proper record, unless Your Honours told us that was not necessary. But in order to go through all the different parts of case, it may take a little bit longer than one might think, if the Defence is going to challenge everything. And that we don't know. We don't know what the Defence intends to do. If their challenges were more specific with regards to very specific parts of the case, it could go much more quickly, but that is not what I would expect. So it could end up taking longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, how long is set aside for the last witness? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I believe that it's -- I believe that it's an hour -- an hour total, half for each side. It may -- we intend to introduce a group of documents, approximately, 85 documents through the witness. I don't think that -- but we're not going to go through each one. It's a batch of documents from an archive. We have spoken to the Defence. The Defence do not object to the admission of these documents. Of course, we'll argue about the weight and how they should be interpreted, but I don't think the admission will take very long. We will lay the foundation for where they came from and so forth, establish authenticity. So it may take a little longer than half an hour, but I think it will take a session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We shall start at 8.00 tomorrow morning and see how things develop. So you're up now next, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I trust you are well rested.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I have on the screen a photograph, 65 ter 03017. Colonel, do you see a photograph there on your screen?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Is it possible for this photograph to be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, do you recognise this area?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hrasnica. It's Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well. With the assistance of the usher, if I ask you to, can you mark on the photograph the location of the house where you were staying and which was damaged as a result of the air bomb explosion?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking for a reference. There was a nulla; and along that nulla, there was a line of houses, but I cannot find that nulla.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Nulla, do you mean small street?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nulla is a small water channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Small water channel, did you say?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm not fully sure, but generally I feel that it should be somewhere -- if that is the line, maybe somewhere here in this line, if that water stream is in this direction. So I can't recognise the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay. So would your house be to the -- let's say, to the left or the right of that line, as we're looking at the photograph?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Would your house to be the left or right of that line that you have just drawn?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look it on the upper side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you see the Igman or the convoy road there on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you mark that, please.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I'd like also to indicate the location of the observation -- the French observation point that we spoke about on Friday, or at least in the rough direction as far as --

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should be somewhere in this area. It was closer to the start of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you know roughly how -- in metres how high the observation point was from --

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was higher than the houses. A little higher than the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That is the examination-in-chief Mr. President. Could I ask that that photograph be tendered and admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P636, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm sorry. I just want to make sure that the evidence was recorded properly and perhaps ask the witness to put the figures OP by the cross, lest it is lost in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, very well. He can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, sorry. I said that you had finished. The cross --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Prosecutor simply wants the Colonel to put a cross somewhere. We can't object to the cross being put.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I made the same request, I was told that it was too late because it had already been tendered into evidence. So I'm afraid it's a question of double standards here, isn't it? I once tendered a photograph and then I asked the photograph to be annotated afterwards, and Judge Harhoff told me that it was too late, which I accepted. I accepted what the Honourable Judge had told me, but it seems to me that we are faced with the same situation here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I don't recollect it, but Judge Harhoff says he has a recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: To my recollection, Mr. President, I understand the situation is little bit different. What I can do is simply say that the cross that is marked on this photograph is the location of the observation point that the witness had spoken about in his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Would you confirm that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. My name is Branislava Isailovic. I'm a lawyer working for the Paris Bar Association, and I represent Mr. Dragomir Milosevic before this Chamber. I shall ask you a few questions concerning your testimony on Friday and this morning. I shall also ask you a few questions about your statement, a statement which you gave to the Prosecutor on the 10th of August, 1996. First of all, I would have liked to see the same photograph, the one which we finished off with, P636.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would like you to turn to this photograph and tell me - and I would like the usher to assist you - I would like you to draw an arrow and indicate in which direction Ilidza is.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. And after 12, 13 years ago, I will try and reply all the answers -- all the questions that you're going to ask me. I'm not 100 per cent correct. It may be a little right or left, and it may not be right according to the scale. But generally what I recollect I will try an answer. This is Hrasnica, if that is the end. So towards this side would be the Ilidza, further left -- sorry, further right as I look at the picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: To be sure, the direction indicates -- the arrow indicates the direction of Ilidza; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you now please be so kind as to mark this with the letter I at the end of the arrow, the area which indicates the direction of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, then, that the Ilidza area is in a valley, in a plain?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: According to your recollection, could you indicate with an arrow in which direction Butmir is, because you also mentioned Butmir.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And could you mark this with a letter B, please.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So this is in the same direction as the first arrow; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Is this in the same direction as Sokolovic Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kolonija, I am not really sure; Sokolovic, yes, was close by. Sokolovic, Butmir, yes; and further left was the Ilidza. From the post, if we see, the left most is Ilidza; and then we have Butmir and Sokolovic on the track going from Hrasnica to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In the same direction as the arrow goes, the one which is marked with the letter B, is that also where the airport is?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, almost in the same direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, at the time, had you been told that there was a tunnel there, and that either the entrance or the exit was close to the airport and therefore close to Butmir?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- from Hrasnica, it was on the other side of the -- other side of the air strip and not so very close, but generally that was the direction we never used. We never went to that place. But generally I know there was probably some tunnel in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, on Friday, you mentioned this observation post which you marked on the photograph. That's where you went in the evening or at night to observe Ilidza, Butmir, and Hrasnica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. It was generally in the evening, evening and maybe then coming late at night. The timings were not fixed, right? Certainly it wasn't in the morning. It was in the afternoon, late afternoon, and then late, not late night; normally, two to three hours. Maybe starting right up to 10.00, 12.00, and then it could be a little earlier and then three, four hours. So the times were not fixed. We would go there and stay there for three, four hours and then come back. But it was in the evening and night, not in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, when you were at the observation post, were you ever able to observe movements of the ABiH army through Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: ABiH, as a convoy or as individuals? Are you asking me as a troop or just individual moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this depends on what you were able to see. Please tell us what you were able to see from the observation post?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as a group or as a company or battalion; but individual movement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned what was called the convoy route. Were you able to see any movement of the ABiH units along this road?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said no, not in the army vehicles. I had seen some of the soldiers, maybe using the other civil trucks but not as a convoy. Maybe one and then a few, two, three, four going probably -- I mean, this is what I think. It may be incorrect also. Somebody coming from the upper positions staying there in Hrasnica and going back. That could be the one, but not as organised movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You went to Hrasnica on the 1st of May, 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And with the Prosecution, you mentioned an incident that occurred on the 1st of July, 1995, an incident in which you were a victim; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Before the 1st of July, you conducted several inquiries on the falling of mortar shells and air bombs?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mortar shell, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You yourself -- well, did you conduct the investigation yourself?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Hrasnica. I think it was in Butmir probably; Butmir or Sokolovic. Butmir, I think it is. It was only on the mortar shell, not the other type of fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can we say, then, that the sole experience with air bombs was on the 1st of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please say again. I'm sorry. I didn't get your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Your sole experience with this air bomb, this projectile, was on the 1st of July, 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. This was on 1st of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, on the 1st of July, you didn't actually see this projectile fall on the house, did you?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just felt it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you heard a noise, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You have described this noise. I would have liked you to say more about it. I feel it is important. You are felt that something big was coming towards you. What did this sound like?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was like a rocket or like the fighter aircraft. It was a loud, not whistling, but loud engine on a fighter aircraft, you could say. It could be one of closer example.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And how long did this last, according to your recollection? This happened a long time ago. For how long did you hear this sound?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twelve seconds [sic].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I see, "12 seconds." You said several seconds.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just a few seconds. I am not very sure. I cannot say one or two or three seconds. I'm not very sure, but a very, very short time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you didn't take part in the investigation which was conducted by the police and by your colleagues from UNMO on the location where the damage was caused and where this projectile exploded.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was evacuated to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: After that, did you come back to this place?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Sarajevo, I think after that treatment I had few stitches. So I stayed there for three, four, five days, and one of the team in Sarajevo. Sierra Golf was probably the name of that team. And in the meantime, this team, they had moved from this place to another location. They had another house in Sokolovic. So when I came back, I reported there and not into that house. So I went twice, thrice to see that place.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I would like you to have another look at the photograph you have before you, Witness. Could you please indicate where the house is, approximately; in other words the area, because there were several houses that were damage. Could you indicate to us where the area was, the area where these damaged houses were, including yours. Just draw a circle around this area please. Can you put a wider circle to indicate the area. I don't want you to mark any particular house.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I'm not very sure. Maybe it was there, if that is the nulla. I'm not very sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just write in 1st of July, 1995 next to this circle? That is the date of the incident.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- now that have you the photograph in front of you, do you remember whether there were any units of the ABiH army in Hrasnica; albeit, ABiH headquarters?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I haven't visited any of the units, but there was one captain, the other day I also told, who used to come us and used to say he was staff officer in somewhere in that area. But I have not visited there. Captain Mustafa was his name. That is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And he was a BiH army captain, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This Captain Mustafa, he was an ABiH army -- ABiH army captain, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a captain. Basically, I mean, as far as the UNMOs were concerned, there was a police officer who normally used to visit us for our welfare or something, asking us, well, [indiscernible] in that area. So at times, I'm not very sure, but maybe two, three time, one of the officer, he came with him, and he was captain -- well, he was from that army, and he has visited our UNMO accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned, if you'll remember, this policeman who visited you on the 1st of July in the evening. So do you remember that evening that a group of people, of whom we do know whether they were military, went to the location where the incident took place; and on that occasion, they threatened you and your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told later, after the incident. I mean, after that explosion, when there was confusion and we were injured, I was told that, yes. There were certain people who -- from that local area. They came running. Probably they were trying to loot that house. I think they took away one of two jerrycans of diesel, and they were asking for money and they were drunk. This is what I was told. I was in hospital. Later on, I was told by my friend that this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And did your colleagues tell you that they had been negatively impressed by those people who came to loot the house?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negatively what?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Impressed.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll say yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I should use another word because in French being impressed by something is a synonym of being frightened, frightened of something. So were they scared of these locals who went to that place after the incident?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, I mean, before the incident, there was no problem. They were very friendly. We were absolutely okay in that area. I mean, everybody was very cooperative, whether it was the organisation or the local people. But after that incident, and on that night, I think the drunk people, they came and they tried to snatch certain things and take certain things from that UNMO house. I think I will say that, yes, to some extent, they were frightened, my colleagues. It was all dark, and we were injured. We were being evacuated, and at that time somebody comes and gets in your house. It has horrible effects.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And did your colleagues tell you that one of them had 12 Canadian dollars stolen from him and 500 German marks?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact amount, but definitely yes. It was Captain Mark or some Canadian captain.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, one of the differences between UNMO and UNPROFOR was that you and your colleagues were not carrying weapons. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And those people who came, according to your colleagues, were they carrying arms?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm. They were without them, I think, and they were just trying to force their way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you'll remember last Friday the Prosecutor tendered a document through you. I'm going to submit it to you, and I'm going to submit it to the Chamber as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that, Your Honour, I would like to tender into evidence this photograph, which has been marked and which is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D184, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now look at document 2770, which has become P635. It is a 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So this is the document, and could you look at page 3. And at the very top, you can see the amounts Captain Hache said were stolen from him. He is a Canadian captain, and we were talking about soldiers. We're told that these were BiH army soldiers.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I said -- you want me to reed the first two, three lines?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: No. I just wanted to show you the amount of money your colleague said was stolen from him, so as to prevent any misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twelve Canadian; US dollar 3.50; 500 Deutschemarks, yes. Is that correct? The black wallet contained about 12 Canadians, 3.50 dollars US, and 500 marks, yes. I said I'm not really sure but, yes, this is correct what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the same time, other things were stolen from your team; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And, Witness, you said that you did not go back to Hrasnica yourself. You said that you found a house in Sokolovici, and you may know that another UNMO -- do you know whether another UNMO team remained in Hrasnica or not?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think it was only our team, and we just shifted our location. There was no other team in Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And how do you explain these facts? As of the 1st -- or between the 1st of May and the 1st of July, were you able to see that military activities from Hrasnica stepped up, became more intense?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said from -- well, that was the time when we had the maximum shelling. That was the time probably the war was right on its peak. But if you say there was certain activities right in the Hrasnica, I haven't observed. Yes, I have seen the individual soldiers moving here and there, and coming, even using that convoy road, but not as a group -- or I mean, a bigger force. Not as a bigger force.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, my first question is: What was exactly your observation mission? Were you there to observe mortar shellings, mortar fire, or were you also to observe any type of firing and armed troop movements as well.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it was any type of firing and any type of movement. That was to be observed; that was the task. It was not restricted to one particular weapon or a particular task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to come back to the Defence counsel questions. Do you confirm that you had never observed troop movements in your area, except some individual soldier movement? If this is the case, there is this report talking about large groups of people and people wearing BiH uniforms. How do you account for that in that case?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm, sir, what I said earlier. I have not seen in the bigger force, say a company 30, 40, 50 or more people together, travelling in a convoy or moving from place one to place two. I confirm that I haven't seen that. What -- as well as that incident is concerned, yes, the people were more, but they were not the army personnels. They were some of them, maybe one, two, three; and some of them, even in that area, they were wearing the uniform. They also used to wear uniform, one-odd people, and would roam about in that area. I think they were locals. Maybe I'm the one that has been referred one or two or three. They are the uniformed person; and, as I know, they had gone to the different places on the -- their fighting places. They used to come back, stay a night, go back again. So maybe these are those people who have come for that night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you also, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Colonel, when you were injured on the 1st of July, you were taken from Hrasnica to Sarajevo. How did you get to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, initially, I was shifted from my location, Hrasnica house, to a local hospital; whereas, I was given the first aid and then it was difficult. I said that the firing was on that track from Hrasnica to Sarajevo. It used to be fired upon any movement on that, so I had to wait for one APC, which had to come from -- it was a French APC which came from Sarajevo, took us from that hospital, myself and the other UNMO from Bangladesh. We both had to move on that, and we had to wait I think two, three hours. I reached hospital at about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So you're saying that the transportation from Hrasnica to Sarajevo had to be done in an armoured vehicle. My next question, therefore, is how did the civilian population move from Hrasnica to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it was a normal local transport, and it was a risky affair. They used to move fast. They used to select the timings when the fire was comparatively less or the observation was less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific. I mean, does that mean during cease-fire periods, or does it mean only at night. So can you explain to us how the civilian population managed to move between Hrasnica and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as I said, it wasn't a normal practice that you would use the APC every time. Late on that night, it was firing so they did not want to take risk. That is number one. Number two is we also used to move, and we used to move on this vehicle and the armoured vehicle that we were otherwise given by the UN. The civilians, they used to move their own vehicle. It was a risky affair. They used to move fast. That that's all. I had not say they should take any precaution, like using the APC or something. They were not provided. But movement was there. It was only normal transport, the local transport and their personal transport, but they used to take risk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Were There any roadblocks on the way?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. There was no planned roadblocks. It was just a -- I'll not say a very good track. It wasn't a road. It was a damaged road, I would say. You can't move very fast on that. Certainly the track was there, but there was no planned barriers on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly if what you're saying is that if you were able to move fast enough in a private car, and if you knew that there was for instance a cease-fire or something, then there would be better chances of getting from one place to the other from Hrasnica to Sarajevo without too much of a risk.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, I just want you to confirm something for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could we try again to have the English interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I can repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, I want you to confirm something for me. In response to, firstly, Defence counsel, just a little bit of time ago, with respect to the incident and what happened after put to you that there were a group of BiH soldiers; and following on from that question, His Honour Judge Mindua also asked you whether -- whether you could confirm that you didn't see troop movements, and if this is the case, there is this report talking about large groups of people and people wearing BiH uniforms. I just want to confirm, if we go back to the document, which is, it's 65 ter 25770. I understand it has an exhibit number, but I'm not -- it's P635, and we could go to page three, please. Colonel, do you see page 3 of your left-hand side of the screen?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If you go down from the top to line 6 -- from the top down to line 6, it's the sentence that starts: "At this time, a large group of locals were milling about in the area." It's the sixth line down from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can we scroll back up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, do you see that sentence there?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At this time, a large group of locals were milling about in the area."

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It says: "At this time, a large group of locals were milling about in the area." And then it goes on: "A soldier then arrived, affronted Captain Hache. He yelled something that was not understood by Captain Hache. He was dressed in an BiH uniform."

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So can you confirm that, in at least with respect to this paragraph, it does not speak about a group of BiH soldiers, does it?

utterances.speaker: IJAZ HUSSAIN MALIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said. It wasn't -- the situation was that we were -- the house was damaged. The people around, they haven't had things to eat. They were rushing into our house, so as to get everything from that house. It was -- it was combination of civilians; maybe one or do we call it sentry or something, who is roaming in that area; maybe a civilian in that ABiH uniform, and maybe one odd, yes, it could be this was also. It is not -- the entire group was not the soldiers. It was a combination of civilians and maybe one-odd soldier, the soldier who had come back from that area, from their defences. This is what I feel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Colonel, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your name, and tell us what you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: My knave is Ewa Tabeau. I'm a demographer. I'm project leader in the Demographic Unit, Office of the Prosecutor OTP, ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court in a few words what it is that a demographer does.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Demographic is a broad area. I have been working for the last seven years in the area of the demography of conflict. This is a very special area of demography. In this area, here at the ICTY, we produce statistics, population statistics, related to consequences of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia from the 1990s; in particular, we have done a lot of work on Bosnia-Herzegovina and other areas. We produce expert reports, like the one we made for this case, which are often tendered into evidence and presented in ICTY cases. Our role is to produce numbers that are as reliable as possible and describe consequences of this conflicts; and in this way, we provide background information about the population suffering during the conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you. And you mentioned in your answer the preparation of expert reports. Did you, at the request of the Prosecutors in this trial, prepare a demographic report concerning civilians killed and wounded in Sarajevo between August of 1994 and November of 1995?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. We made this report on the request from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And is that a copy of the report that is on the witness stand with you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. That -- this is the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this report was accepted into evidence by the Chamber in a decision dated 4th of April, 2007. Could it please be assigned an exhibit number at this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P637, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: One moment, please, Your Honour. For the record, Your Honour, that was 65 ter 03127.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, in preparing this report, did you investigate the number of people killed through war-related causes in Sarajevo between August of 1994 and November of 1995?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. This is one of the statistics that we produced and included in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I want to ask you some clarifying questions before we get to the numbers themselves. First of all, I'm using the term "Sarajevo." Precisely, what geographic area did you take in your report as being synonymous with Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Sarajevo is an area that is composed of ten municipalities, in the broad sense, and there is also another area composed of six municipalities, which is the most central part of Sarajevo. People tend to say "Sarajevo" in the context of this smaller area, and we studied both areas. The Sarajevo Six -- the term "Sarajevo Six" is used for the smaller area of six municipalities of Sarajevo, and the Sarajevo Ten is the broader area. In the case of Sarajevo Ten, some of the municipalities were entirely or partly behind the front lines in Sarajevo. But the Sarajevo six is the central area studied in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, secondly, what period of time exactly did you study in preparing this report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: We studied actually for context to all purposes, for reference purposes, the entire conflict starting April 1992 to November 1995. But for this particular case, for the Dragomir Milosevic case, we studied the period starting in August 1994 to November 1995, and statistics relevant to this case were compiled according to period, August 1994/November 1995 and the Sarajevo Six area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Let's turn, first, to the question of deaths, and the first question concerning the study of deaths is: What exactly the method was that you were following. Did you attempt to actually count all deaths, or did you take a sample and then extrapolate from that to get the overall number?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: We were actually in a very exceptional situation source-wise, so we could afford to produce statistics that can be seen as results of an accounting approach, as opposed to the extrapolation approach. Extrapolation is usually based on a sample based on which certain numbers, statistics are produced. But in our report about the killed persons, we actually tried to count them, as many as we could identify in our sources. Simply speaking, sources were good enough to go for the accounting approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, you have mentioned a couple of times in that answer the sources you had and how good these sources were. Could you give us a summary of the sources that you had at your disposal, and then we will go through them one at a time and talk about what those sources are and how thorough their coverage was. But to begin, could you just summarize the sources for us please?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The three major sources that we used for the statistics on the killed persons include the databases, mortality databases, compiled by, in first case, the statistical authority of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Second source is a similar mortality database established by the statistical authority of the Republika Srpska. These two sources jointly cover 140.000 death records from the conflict period, starting April 1992 to November -- actually, even, December 1995, and include both natural deaths -- records of natural deaths and also records of war-related deaths. War-related deaths are marked, are flagged in this databases, based on the documentation that was available to the statistical authority. So it was decision that actually came to us together with the original sources. These two sources are quite exceptional. They are big. They are reliable because established by professional statisticians, and both were established used standardised forms; questionnaires, the so-called death notification questionnaires; the respondents who were the close relatives of the deceased --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I'm too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I am sorry. Could I interrupt for just one moment. First of all, I think the interpreters would appreciate if could you slow your rate of speech just a little bit. Second of all, I was wondering if you might also be able to tell us, briefly, what the other sources were that you had reference to, and then we will come back and do a more thorough exposition of each source, once we have got them are all out on the table?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So once, again, major sources include two mortality databases; one by FBiH statistical authority, one by RS statistical authority. In addition to these two, we use the ICRC List of Missing Persons, 2005 Edition. In addition to these three major sources, we used smaller sources and -- well, sources that were not established by professional statisticians. I'm speaking of the Bakije Funeral Home business records and about the Sarajevo Household Survey from mid-1994. Bakije Funeral Home is the largest and oldest funeral home that has burying Muslims in Sarajevo. So most Muslims, if not all, are buried in this particular funeral home. The Sarajevo Household Survey is a survey conducted by mid-1994, by a research institute from Sarajevo, a survey that is very large, covering 75.000 households living in Sarajevo by mid-1994. We used these sources covering both the records of killed persons and also the records of wounded persons. So even though we didn't use this particular one for the estimates of the killed persons, we still did use these particular source for our estimate of the wounded persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: But this is not all, let me finish. This is the list of sources that were directly used to produce statistics. But because of reporting of military status is incomplete and generally poor in several sources, we decided, in addition to these major sources, to use three lists of fallen military personnel from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina; the list of ABiH fallen personnel, VRS fallen personnel, HVO fallen personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Let's start at the stop of those sources. You mentioned two statistical sources compiled by governmental bodies. One was compiled by the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. One was compiled by the statistical authorities of the Republika Srpska. How were those compiled, and how were they useful to you in preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I started speaking about this already, so these are databases established on reporting of deaths. That is normally done in every country and is part of vital events statistical information system. The two databases were established actually on our request of the OTP request by these both authorities. They used -- the statistical authorities used a standardised questionnaire to collect the information from the relatives, the so-called death notification questionnaire. The questionnaire is attached in the annex to this report. The Informants or the persons from whom the information was obtained were the close, very close relatives of the persons reported, so the information in the forms is reliable to the extent, of course, the families remember details of the deceased but usually they do. The design of this databases is very professional. Databases were cleaned by professional statisticians. Responses in the databases have been standardised. So the quality of information that we have in this databases is very high. However, these two databases, even though very good, are still incomplete. The coverage is not full. We know that parts of information, relevant information, is not there, and this is related to the fact that not all families were able to report the deaths in time. Usually, there is a short period of three days for doing this. And part of the documentation was destroyed in the war as well. ICRC List of Missing Persons is an another source --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, before you go to the ICRC List of Missing Persons, were you able to get an idea of how incomplete or the extent of the lack of completion of the two statistical databases, and how did you go about doing that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is very hard to establish the incompleteness of these sources, especially of these sources. We know that all existing documentation from the territory practically of entire country has been computerised, and it is in these databases. The number of records of 144.000 is also high. It higher than normally would be expected if there was no conflict at all, but the difference is not that large. We are aware of many, many more victims than what we see as an extra axis of mortality in these two databases. So incompleteness must be counted in thousands; not a few thousand, but many, many thousands of deaths that are not there. Some of them are missing persons. The list of 22.000 individuals reported to the ICRC could not be reported to the statistical authorities, as the bodies of many of them are still not identified. So as long as there are bodies not identified and there is no death declaration, it is impossible to include such a person in statistics, simply speaking. This is why we decided to include the list of missing persons as the third major source.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I think you anticipate my next question, which is to describe, please, the role that the ICRC database of missing persons played in your analysis, especially in filling in information that might otherwise might not have been available from anywhere else. Could do you that, please?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, as I said, records of missing persons are just additional to the records of known deaths. Records of known deaths in the two major databases are the FBiH databases. Missing persons are on the list of missing persons. In Sarajevo, missing persons were not that frequent, compared with other episodes of the conflict, like Srebrenica for instance. But we still did it for completeness and for obtaining as large coverage as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then you mentioned this in a couple of answers ago. But now that you have got a list of dead and missing presumed dead people, how do you go about making sure -- since your brief was to look into the number of civilian deaths, how do you go about making sure that you're not counting a killed soldier as a killed civilian, or vice verse counting a killed civilian as a killed soldier? How did you approach that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is an important issue; because in the major sources, the reporting of military status is incomplete and efficient. So using the original -- and in some sources, there is no information about military status at all, like, for instance, in the ICRC list of missing person. In other sources for some individual, there is record of a military unit a person belonged to but. That's all we have. Based on this, it would be very unreliable to produce statistics on civilians killed verses soldiers killed in the siege. Well, we decided, therefore, to use the three lists of fallen military personnel in the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Three's three lists jointly cover for the entire conflict and entire country about 48.000 records. The main group of individuals reported in these three military lists are army members, but also police members are included and there is also personnel of Ministry of Defence included, as well as individuals who were involved in production section -- sector providing services and goods to the army. But we still did use this list knowing that the number of military personnel reported in these three list is probably a little bit too high. These were not only soldiers who died in combat, but also other individuals associated with the armies in this or that way. We used these lists as a reference source. We compared records on these three lists with the master list that we compiled and on sources that we decided to use for producing statistics, and marked the records on our master list the records found in the military lists, as soldiers, as military personnel. In addition to this, to be on the safe side and to be conservative, we still kept any individual marked as a military person, as a soldier. In the original sources, we kept this person marked as a military person. So we didn't change this reporting. So we, simply speaking, created a variable, an item that was measuring, and I think it was quite a good measure of the military status, civilians versus soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, we have talked about the three, I believe you say, main databases that you used; the two governmental statistical databases plus the ICRC's List of Missing Persons. But there were two other databases that you used. The first being the Sarajevo Household Survey. To begin with, could you just explain to us what you is the Sarajevo Household Survey, and then I will have some questions about how it was used in your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Sarajevo Household Survey is a large survey conducted in the spring and summer of 1994, so practically earlier than the indictment period of the Dragomir Milosevic case begins. And this survey covers -- in principle it was meant as a complete survey, so it was meant to cover all population, all households living in Sarajevo within the front lines by mid-1994. All together we estimated that the population, in terms of individuals covered by the survey, amounted to approximately 340.000 individuals, which is about 75 per cent of the settled population in Sarajevo in 1991, in the Sarajevo Six area. That means it was a large survey. It is a survey, although not run by statisticians, professional statisticians, but still by researchers, and it is a survey based on a standardised questionnaire, in which we have actually a full information about victims in terms of individuals with names, date of birth, with -- sorry, year of birth, and information about whether or not a person was killed or wounded. So it is a quite an extensive and large survey. Reliability is perhaps not as high -- as good as in the RS and FBiH mortality databases, but it is still quite acceptable for this kind of analysis that we prepared in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And who -- you say this was not prepared by professional statisticians. Do you know who it is was that did conduct the Sarajevo Household Survey?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. It was a group of researchers working in the institute for I think -- I don't remember the name of the institute, but I think in the section number 2, where the sources discussed -- the name of the institute is mentioned in full, and this is the Institute for Research of War Crimes and International Law. The institute was led at that time by Professor Smail Cekic. I think Smail Cekic is still there also today, and he has done not only this survey but also several other surveys. Well, I think they produced some results that can be seen as meaningful.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now that we have a sense of what the Sarajevo Household Survey was, could you tell us what role it played in the statistical and demographical analysis that you conducted for this trial?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The Household Survey, as I said, was not used for producing statistics on the killed person. We used this survey in other estimates of the number of persons wounded in the siege. The survey is exceptional because of its size and because of the fact that covers wounded persons, both hospitalised and not hospitalised. That means it gives a much better impression of the size of the wounding process in Sarajevo. When compared with, for instance, hospital admission records, that only covers patients with the most serious injuries and wounding, who are admitted to hospital for treatment. So it is good source to be used to together with other sources, based on which we could make an estimate, an extrapolation of the number of persons wounded in the siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. And then, lastly, you mentioned the business records of Bakije Funeral Home in Sarajevo. Can you tell us, please, why you used those business records and what role those records wound up playing in your statistical analysis of killed persons?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, this is yet another additional sources, reporting on the killed persons. Well, in situations like the siege of Sarajevo, the situation occasionally became very chaotic and people were killed on the streets sometimes in large numbers. These funeral home guys, the Bakije Funeral Home, was very active in burying bodies found on the streets. They just were collecting bodies often under fire -- being under fire and buried the bodies. Often they looked for families of the individuals and actually notified the families of the losses. And as I said, there is no source in conflict situation that is complete 100 per cent. So the more sources can be used, the better for the completeness of produced statistics. This is the main reason that we decided to use the records of the funeral home. In addition, it's a large source. It contains approximately 12.000 records for the conflict period from April 1992 to December 1995, which is a lot, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The last question I have regarding these sources is to ask you to pleas explain to Their Honours how it is that you avoided double counting; and if someone was listed in both, let's say, the federal statistical database and the Bakije Funeral Home database, how did you make sure that you counted them once and not twice?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, we applied here our standard methodology, which always included as part of our standard procedure for any source. First of all, checking sources one by one and checking whether or not there are in the duplicates in the sources. Whatever duplicates are found are then eliminated in a single source, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Counsel, how would the witness discover if it was a duplicate?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That's the question I had thought I put to the witness. Maybe it wasn't that clear. Dr. Tabeau, the hypothetical example I gave was a person was listed both in one of the statistical databases and in the funeral home database, and the question pending was how do you make sure that person gets counted once not twice.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. Comparing records involves comparing a number of data items available from every record. If there are two persons reported in two sources, the persons are characterised by names; first name, father' name, surname, date of birth, place of birth; and then another portion of information is the information about the death or wounding, including date of the event, place of the event, causes of the event. In searching for duplicates, we compare the personal information; that means name, first name, surname, father's name, and date of birth. And if we find records that have identical or very similar value in this four fields, then we study the remaining part of the information, the information about the event. Based on the results of this comparison, we declare a person, a record, to be a duplicate, one or not. That is basically the methodology. Methodology is just comparing relevant pieces of information related to possibly the same individuals listed on different lists. I hope that is a clear answer. But there are more issues than just the issue of comparing certain pieces of information. Names, for instance, are often misspelled. Pieces of date of birth are missing. There is also a possibility that date of birth is reported differently in different sources. So the borderline related to when one can accept a pair of related records as a duplicated record and when not is sometimes very hard to find indeed. But because the sources main sources were of high quality, these comparisons were not as hard as one might think they were hard. Actually, it was, I think, not such a big issue here, the elimination of the duplicates. But I was trying to say is there are several aspects of looking for duplicates. On one level, these are the duplicates within the sources, source by source. This often happens that even one single source reports on one person several times. So, first of all, duplicates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- do you have a separate, discreet exercise to discover double counting, or is it something that you just come upon fortuitously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Discreet exercise, I mean, on whether I have a number? What do you mean? Is it terms of discretion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, not discretion. Discreet means separate. Do you have an individual, independent exercise to discover double counting, or is it something that you discover as incidental to your other statistical work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a major part of our work. 90 per cent of our work is checking duplicates. When sources are combined, like we did for this project, sources are met. When sources are met together, then we have an additional problem; not only duplicate within sources, source by source, but we also have an overlap of sources. So if a master list is created, based on a number of sources, then what has to be done at that stage is yet another exercise for -- of looking for duplicates, because the overlap of the sources must eliminated. This is what we do most of our time, and there is a unit. There are three persons who are fully skilled to do this kind of work, and we've doing this for several years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We have passed the time for the break, so we will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, just a couple of things before we go on. First of all, I was ways approached at the break and asked to please remind you to speak a little bit more slowly. This is very dense and technical material you're testifying about, and I know that can be hard to bear in mind because you are fight properly focussed on the substance of your testimony. So I hope will you not be offended if every once in a while I give you a friendly reminder. And in a second matter, in doing a final, final check of the report before coming to Court, did you find some typographical errors?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I. I made a list of things that needed to be corrected, but most of them are typos. There are also two more specific corrections, like one major report, expert report, that we made in the past is not on the list of our expert reports. Well, one number must be corrected, but none of these corrections change the substance of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: We have -- we have made copies of the list that you prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could I please ask that those be distributed at this time, so that everyone can take a look at them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your testimony, Dr. Tabeau, just to repeat, is that none of this, in the errata sheet, would change the substance of the report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I want to move on, then, to the topic that we were covering just before the break, which was number of killed persons from war-related activities in Sarajevo during the indictment period. And I want to refer to tables 8A, 8B, 9A, and 9B, which appear in your report, beginning on page 23 of the English version and continuing to page 24. And for convenience, we have put those on a power point slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I will ask Ms. Bosnjakovic to please pull up slide number one and broadcast it within the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, do you see that on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: What is this screen for? Can I have that table and the transcript at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: To be begin with, Dr. Tabeau, we see this division again between Sarajevo Six and Sarajevo Ten. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. It's correct. Perhaps I should list or mention the municipalities that are included in Sarajevo Six. This is Sarajevo Centar, Ilidza, Novi Grad, Novo Sarajevo, Stari Grad, and Vogosca. This is the area of the Sarajevo Six. The area of the Sarajevo Ten, in addition to the six, we have also Sarajevo Hadzici, Ilijas, Pale, and Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, I notice that for both Sarajevo Six and Sarajevo Ten, you've got two minimum numbers. One is called absolute and one is called more likely. I want to be begin with the minimum number absolute. What does that number respect, and why is it called the absolute minimum number?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This number is the very, very minimum, absolute minimum number obtained from the merged sources, that would be the FBiH, RS, ICRC List of Missing, and Bakije Funeral Home lists. These are the records that can be seen and are documented in the sources as violent, war-related deaths. These records were marked by the statistical authorities as resulting from the so-called war activities. War activities cover a whole broad change of situations, certainly situations in which people were killed by fire-arms, different types of fire-arms, or they died another type of violent war-related death. These deaths for which we have extensive information about their violent war-related character, and the information comes from the documentation available to the owners of the sources. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: -- minimum numbers, if I may continue, don't include cases which are indirectly related to war. All these indirect war-related deaths are included in another component. Natural deaths are not recorded here in the statistics. Also unknown causes of death, case of unknown causes of death are excluded from these first kind of statistic absolute minimum number. The number of unknown -- of cases with unknown causes was, however, relatively big. In the case of Sarajevo Six, this number was more than one thousand deaths. So we thought it was really important to give an impression of what the statistics would look like if a part of the cases with unknown causes would be included in statistics. It's pretty sure that among the cases with unknown causes of death, a number of cases were from natural causes and a number were from violent war-related causes. There are statistical techniques that can be used to estimate these two components and this is what we did. This is why the second minimum number is included in these tables, and we call this number a more likely minimum number. I want to stress that both numbers, the absolute minimum and the more likely minimum, are still minimum numbers, at least numbers. That means they are by no means complete, and there is number of deaths still somewhere there that we were unable to count and to include in statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So, Dr. Tabeau, just for the record, as the demographer who prepared this expert report, what is the number of civilians who were killed in Sarajevo Six as a result of violent, war-related causes between August of 1994 and November of 1995?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This number is 449. This is the absolute minimum number. But more likely, I believe, we believe, that the minimum number is 659 deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then the same for the Sarajevo Ten, how many civilians were killed as a result of violent, war-related causes between August of 1994 and November of 1995?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: An absolute minimum is 631, and a more likely minimum number is 915.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the question of calculating the number of people wounded as a result of war-related activities. In --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: One moment. Just a minute, Prosecutor, before moving on to another topic and before talking about the wounded, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I request your assistance, please. I want transcript on my screen. I'm sorry for this. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have listened very carefully to everything you have said so far; and as far as Sarajevo Six is concerned, you mentioned that there were unknown causes of death that might have been due to road accidents or diseases or crimes or other reasons. You also said that deaths were caused by shells and caused by the war for the main part in your testimony. Before the break, you stated that you avoided double counting and counting one death twice. So this is my question: With the technique you use, is it possible to know whether an unknown cause of death or a natural cause of death, like a disease, could that be accounted for or introduced in your records? Could it be considered to have been caused by the war by rocket fire or by a mortar shell? In other words, with the statistical data you use, and given the way you work, is it possible to avoid such a thing happening? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that I understand the question, although it is very complex. I think it is important that we will -- I will talk a little bit about the methodology. We actually spent quite sometime earlier today on speaking about the sources, but I didn't explain the method we used for producing these statistics. I want to begin with the information that in all these sources individual records of information are available. One case reported in every source represents one individual. Information that we have about individuals is complex. We have information about personal details, like names, date of birth, place of birth, residence, et cetera, and also an extensive part of information is related to the event considered. One type of event we studied was the violent, war-related deaths, the killed persons, and the second event very studied is the wounding event. Every event is characterised by a number of items, by the date, what day and month and year is concluded, by the place of the event. Place is often expressed as a particular place, a small territorial area, and also a place in terms of a larger territorial area, like a municipality, which is an official administrative area. We have also information about causes of death or wounding. Reporting of causes of death might be very complex, and it is very complex. The simplest situation is with the list of missing persons for whom we know that they went all missing, so that would be the cause of the fact that the person is still unaccounted for. But in terms of known deaths, of course, the causes are much more complex, especially that both natural causes and violent, war-related causes are reported. In these two major databases, we asked the authorities who developed these databases to use a medical classification of health conditions, diseases, or accidents that led to death. So the medical classification is available for a vast majority of our deaths. This is just one perspective. The medical perspective is based on the official classification of diseases, causes of death provided systematically by the WHO, World Health Organisation 10th edition. It is used in both databases. So medical causes report about what organ failures led to death. So that is a whole description of how, why the people died because of what organs and what injuries to the organs. There is a table in the report - it is Table 12, as far as I remember. Yes, Table 12 -- in which causes, medical causes of death of the violent war-related deaths are listed. In addition to medical causes, there are two other classifications available for causes of death of known deaths. These are for violent deaths. We have type of violent death. There are five major types. One of them is war activities. Other of the five include accidents, including traffic accidents, other violent deaths include murder, suicide. These would be the major categories. And this was the type of violent death, which is a second perspective. There is a third perspective available as well, and the third perspective tells us for violent deaths what external factors led to that. And the external factors would be whether the person died in fire, was the person poisoned, was the person injured in some kind of circumstances. So this would be the external causes of death. They described the circumstances of death. So regarding causes of death, we have a lot of information that we can use to study and to decide whether or not we can include a given death as a violent, war-related case. And this is had a we did. We studied, first of all, violent deaths, only violent deaths that were marked by the authorities as war-related. That means resulting from war activities. And we neglected completely all natural deaths, which are different from violent deaths. Generally, all deaths are either violent or natural. We concentrated on the violent deaths, and one category was the major category of war related resulting from war activities. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you finished or not yet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really. It is a very long story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we have heard enough, Doctor. Let Judge Mindua continue his questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the explanation you provided. I shall now be much clear, and I hope this will be my last question. Among the sources, you mentioned the Statistical Institute of the Republika Srpska and you also mentioned the BiH Institute. This is my question: I wanted to know whether you were able on looking at all this statistical data, whether it be data coming from the ABiH or the Republika Srpska, did you note any death that came under a heading which you may have found in other sources you used, like the ICRC or the Household Survey which was conducted? Did you see that certain cases were officially due to the war or did you discover that these same people had died in a different way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this question relates to how we dealt with the overlap of sources. It's indeed the one and the same death, one in the same case could be reported in several sources, up to five sources. This is as many as sources as we used for this project. It's important to explain that our intention was to make one master list of death cases, a list that would be based on all individual sources. But merging sources involves issues of which of the overlapping records should be taken for as the only one that remains in the master list, and which ones should be skipped as duplicated. One and the same case, one the same death can be reported in FBiH database, RS database, ICRC database, and Bakije Funeral Home, and which of the four we take for the master list and which ones we decide are do you believe indicated. Knowing that sources are -- some are better, some are less good, we decided to use a hierarchy sources. It was that FBiH and RS databases were considered to be our best sources, and they were consistent in case of duplications that whatever source was used here for just keeping this one single record was okay, whether it was FBiH or RS. Then if saw one the same record, the very same record in addition in other sources, we neglected the other record. So what remains is this one reported in the our best sources. So that is the way we dealt with the overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor. These explanations are difficult to really understand, especially when you come down to the details, so maybe I could put an example to you, and you could to us just how you would handle such an example. Let us say that there is a shelling incident, and one of your most reliable sources will say that 22 persons were killed, the other most reliable source would say that there were only 19 persons killed; and when you then check all the other sources you have, you were able to establish the identity of only 15 of the victims. This would leave you in a very difficult situation, I would assume. Which result would you end up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it is a difficult situation, because depending on which -- the maximum reported, in this incident, is 22 persons, 22 persons. That means even if the 15 would be reported in our best sources, I would, first of all, take the 15. But because it is only 15 in the best sources, and the rest is in less good source, then I would additionally include seven records from other sources. So I wouldn't have more than 22. That is the maximum reported in my sources, but I would not have less or more than 22. I would just have 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
