utterances.text: But chances would be that in fact, in the example that I mentioned, in fact there were only 19 people killed, because one of the reliable sources said 22, the other said 19, and you were only able to establish the identity of 15 of these 19 or 22 people. So there's a small margin here which I just wonder whether you would go on the safe side and say out of this example, we only know for sure that 15 people were killed, or would you go with the middle figure to say that we can establish four sure that at least 19 people were killed, or would you take the bigger number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once again, we have three numbers; 22, 19, and 15, and we have four sources. And just assume that 22 and 19 were reported in the best sources, and the other number, 15, was reported in the least reliable source, the fourth source. How I would deal with this situation. Well, the maximum individuals reported in this one incident is 22 persons. Because the two best sources report a very close number, 22/19, I would certainly compare the 22 with 19. And there is a very good chance that the 19 are exactly the same in the 22, in my first source. So I would still have 22 records after I would have analysed the two sources. So then I would go to the 15 individuals reported in the last source, and I would compare the names of the 15 with the list of 22 I have. And it is very likely that there is again the 15 names included in the 22 already. So I would still have the 22 individuals reported, if there is a consistency among source; if there is not, I may have 15 additional names, 15 additional new names, that I would probably included in my list as well, at this stage. If they are not overlapping name, completely new names, then in addition to the 22, I would have new 15 names. This is what I would do, even though I would know that the 15 names come the least reliable source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm confused, but on a high level. Please, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, let me follow up, if I may, with the question Judge Harhoff was asking. Now, Judge Harhoff put this position that there is a specific shelling incident, and deaths are reported as resulting from that shelling incident. First of all, are deaths in fact reported that way in the sources that you looked at?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Not by shelling incidents. This is not included among the causes. I don't have information about shelling, sniping incidents as causes of death, but I do have information about the time and place. Every incident actually can be quite well approximated by using the information about the time and place of incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And let me follow up on that. It will get better, I promise. Judge Harhoff was also putting to you, for example, that one source might say that 22 people were killed in a shelling on such-and-such a day. In order for a record to be counted, to be included in your master list, what is the minimum that that record has got to have before you will say, Here is a countable death, into the list it goes, and we will check and maybe sure it is not double counted somewhere else, but this is a record that I will include, and which records are so incomplete where you say, No, we just can't even put that in?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, we are required for records to have all names, and that means first name, father' name, surname; and ideally the date of birth, complete date of birth; complete date of incident, ideally, I'm saying; and complete place of incident; and ideally information about cause of death. But this is not what was available for all -- absolutely all records. So as a minimum, we decided to have names, year of birth, and year of death, and the cause of death that was explicitly not natural. That was the minimum that was required for our statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So in a hypothetical situation, in which some source says, and maybe not evenly one of the sources that you use, but somebody says, Wasn't that incident awful. There were 30 people killed; no names, no date of births, no dates of death. Does that claim of 30 people killed on such-and-such a day make into your report or not; and then please give the reasons for your answer.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Of course, if we couldn't have information about place of death and date of death, there is no way we could use this record. This record is useless from the point of view of the work we had done. Well, it was required, as a basic principle, to work with these records which were relevant to the siege area and the siege period of this case. That means the area was the Sarajevo Six, and the date of incidents relevant to the case were from August 1994 to November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: This will the last question on this. In this master list of deaths, are you working from death records or from incident records?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: We are working from death records. We don't have incident data as the basic principle for selecting records into the database. This is not what we had at our disposal, the incidents information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I still have not fully understood, in the example that I mentioned before, how you would handle the data according to which you are using all available sources, reliable and unreliable, you were only able to establish the identity of 15 people, yet your two most reliable sources then told you that there were more deaths. In one source, it would say that they were sure that there were at least 19 deaths; that is to say, four people unidentified. The other source says a slightly higher number, let us for the example just say 22 people. That is one thing. But then if you wish, you may try and explain to the Chamber just how you would handle this information, and how you would establish the number to be entered into your record. The other information that you gave us was that you are using a death approach and not an incident approach. We have heard during this trial that there were numerous incidents of sniping, and I guess that these have been recorded as sniping incidents. In this Chamber, in this trial, we have only heard evidence of a limited number of these sniping incidents. So I assume that apart from the cases that we have heard, the sniping cases that we have heard during this trial, there are a number of other sniping incompetences. Let us assume that there is one single shot fired by a sniper and one person is killed in the street and nothing else; then how would you be able to establish that this person was killed by a sniping incident and not as a casualty of a traffic accident, a simple, normal traffic accident, which would be unrelated to the war? People are killed, of course, in traffic every day. So if you had no attention paid to the incidents, then I have difficulties in understanding how you would be able to distinguish a war-related casualty with a traffic casualty. Could you try to explain this to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I will start with the second part of the question; the person shot by a sniper in the sniping incident. I don't have the information about sniping incident, but I would see this person as killed -- as died, for instance, because of a heart injury; and in the classification of violent deaths, I would see this person as died because of war activity. And if I have a little bit of luck, then in external causes, I see this person as died of a gunshot. I wouldn't see whether it was a sniper, perhaps in some cases I would, but not in all. But I would definitely see that fire-arm was involved. So that is the logic behind this project that we completed. We don't have information about sniping incidents. We don't have information about shelling incidents. We don't have information about any other shooting incidents during the siege, but we do have information about deaths and we do have information about the nature of the deaths. And we are able to distinguish between natural deaths and violent deaths; and among the violent deaths, we are able to distinguish this one particular group of deaths related or resulting from war activities. So it is not this direct approach that ideally we would like to have, beginning from the sniping/shelling incidents and counting the deaths resulting from this. This is not possible because there are no sources that I would how to do this, on the scale that we have done in this report. But we have talk the other end. We have a good reporting of deaths from the siege period and the siege area, and this is quite an exceptional number of sources that we have. And starting from this end, we produce statistics that are if not 100 per cent then, they are in a very large extent certainly reporting on the very same victims from the very same incidents. But the link between the incidents, sniping/shelling, and the deaths yet needs to be made as a direct link. If I would have lists of victims of certain sniping/shelling incidents, I could have searched for them in my master list and check whether they are reported and how they are reported. So this is actually the essence of this report, right, what I said now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What about the first question posed by Judge HARHOFF.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to put a drawing on the ELMO, if I may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have here an example of three sources: Source 1, this is this area; source 2; and source 3. Just imagine we have a project in which we want to make a master list that would be composed of records coming from three sources; one, two, three. Because the sources are related to each other, why, because they report on the same or similar period an area, there must be that the sources are overlapping. And the overlap of sources is a complex issue. This is the overlap all three sources; one, two and three. So this is a group of records that, if I would simply put the three sources together, together means if there N1 one number of records in Source 1, N2 number of records in Source 2, N3 number of records in Source 3, then putting them together means N1 plus N2 plus N3. That is the overall total of just putting them, technically speaking, together, merging them. But the total, N1 plus N2 plus N3, is the wrong total because we know that sources overlap and we have to get rid of a number of records. So this group of records; that is, these cases, are counted three times; one, two, three. They are reported in all sources. This group are records overlapping between two sources; one and two. Here, one and three; here, two and three. So these are counted, too; those are counted, too; and those are counted, too. So my role is to eliminate of every record reported three times. Of every report reported three times, I have to eliminate two and leave just one in the master list. And of all records, reported two times, my task is to keep just one of every two and get rid of the other one. So master list is just combining sources in the good way, getting rid of duplicated records, and coming up with a number of records that can be seen as unique and related to the incidents in question, and show this as statistics. This is what we have done. So coming back to the example: 22, 19 and 15. So depending -- this would be 22; this would be in total 19; and this would be 15. Depending on how they overlap here, how they overlap here, my number can be as large as 22 plus 19 plus 15. That would be the maximum if there no duplicated records at all, at all. So I would just 22 plus 19 plus 15, if no duplicates, or much less than that, much less than that, I think, depending on how they overlap. So that is my answer. I hope it made it a little bit easier to understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is that the best answer can you provide to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this stage, yes, but I can come up with a concrete example with names, in a later time, if it would help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let me move back to your answer to my second question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- about how you distinguish a war-related casualty from a normal casualty. Let's again have an example. We have this little boy walking home from school one day. It's a hot and sunny day, and he is being shot at. The bullet hits him in his arm, and he is taken to hospital. I guess the record would show that he has a broken wrist, the bullet hit him through the wrist. Now, I can see two possibilities. One possibility would be that he is recorded as a victim of a sniping incident; the other would be that he fell on his bicycle and broke his wrist. Where would he end up in your system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not a killed person. It is a wounded person, so we have a case of a wounded person. If was it a serious injury, and it was, he would go to hospital with his mom, and he would be diagnosed there. There would be a file made for him in that hospital. In the hospital, I'm not sure whether he would be admitted or not. Even if he would not be admitted, there is a very good chance the file would be very extensive and complete. And for wounded persons, we have extensive information about shelling and sniping as causes of wounding. This is very different from the information that is available for the killed persons. For killed, we don't have information about shelling or sniping as causes of death. For wounded persons, we do. This is a matter of reporting what is available and reported in the sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm sure I understand. Why would the medical records from hospitals be available to you only for persons that were wounded but not killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because killed persons are not taken to hospital. This is why. Because they are killed and they are not requiring any medical help. They are just dead, so they don't end in hospitals. We don't have admission for the killed persons. If a wounded persons died of the injuries, then for this group we would have the admission file available. But this is only a very small group of individuals. Those first wounded, who didn't recover from the injuries and died of the injuries, for those we would have information about shelling, sniping as causes of wounding. So this is a different source we used for the wounded persons, and this is why the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, what do you see as the significance of Dr. Tabeau's evidence, significance for the case for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau's evidence establishes the number of people killed and wounded as a result of war-related activities during the indictment period and particularly those areas in the Sarajevo Six, which are the areas within the confrontation lines. The Prosecution's view is that this is an absolute minimum number of persons killed or wounded as a result of activities directed by the accused in this case. Dr. Tabeau will not say, of course, that last bit, but the inference is there to be argued, and it certainly will be argued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So in the absence of this kind of evidence, where does that leave your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In the absence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the absence of this kind of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In the absence of this kind of evidence, it leaves us unable to give -- it would leave us unable to give an exact number in terms of casualties suffered as a result of activities perpetrated by the troops under command of the accused and would leave us with anecdotal evidence; for example, police officers saying that there were a lot of calls during the siege period and few following the siege period. It would also leave us, for example, the medical records that were introduced via spreadsheet earlier in the trial, but it would leave us without an exact number and it would leave us without the statistical derivation of that exact number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you need an exact number to prove your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I don't need an exact number. However, I hope we are doing something more than the bear minimum needed to prove the case. The -- the question -- if we went with the bear minimum, that would be a very -- very dodgy approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm just trying to put the evidence in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get it in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, of course, depending on the outcome of the liability phase of the trial, these number could be highly relevant in fixing an appropriate penalty, a sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. It would be relevant there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, I promise, I hope this is last question following up on Judge Harhoff. In Judge Harhoff's example, there were 22, there were 19, there were 15, and I believe Judge Harhoff said there were a number of unidentified people. You have already testified that you have a master list of unique records. Can a wholly, unidentified person have a unique record?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Not in the sources that we used. A record, to be included and considered meaningful, must be fully identified. There must be names and other information about the person. If there would be only cases, reported, dearth cases or wounding cases, without the information about persons, we would reject them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So the answer to my question was, in the example I mentioned, you would end up recording only 15 deaths.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are only 15 with names, then yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm now going to turn to wounded persons, and I'm going to start off the same way I did with the death persons but hopefully a bit quicker, because I understand from the answers that you have already given that your sources were by and large the same, only you also made use of the Household Survey in calculating wounded persons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Actually, the sources were not --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I apologise. I misstated that. The sources for wounded persons, I meant to refer back to the hospital records that you had talked about, were by and large hospital records. Can you tell us what use you made of hospital records in calculating the number of wounded persons?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: So to make it clear once again, our sources for the wounded persons were just different. It was just basically hospital records that we used as the main source for producing the minimum number of the wounded persons. Hospital records came from three major hospitals in Sarajevo; Kosevo, Dobrinja, and State Hospital. The hospital records is a very small sample of records on all wounded persons in the siege of Sarajevo. The only covered persons who were admitted the information comes from admission files of the hospitals; non-hospitalised wounded persons are not covered in this sample, moreover, records from other hospitals, like the war hospitals that operated in Sarajevo during the siege, in addition to these three major hospitals. So the records of war hospitals are not included in our sample. Records from emergency help stations are not included either. So what I'm saying is it is a very small presentation that we have and a very small number of wounded persons, as a minimum number that we can present. However, knowing all this, knowing that the incompleteness is so large, and knowing that the hospital records are just one of the sources that could be used for these kind of analysis, we also tried to improve this minimum number by producing an estimate of a more complete number of all wounded persons, both hospitalised and non-hospitalised. We have done this by including in our analysis one additional source, the Sarajevo Household Survey. The Sarajevo Household Survey, even though the reporting ends in this source by mid-1994, but the period from April 1992 to July 1994 is covered by both hospital records and also Sarajevo Household Survey. By comparing these two sources, especially by studying similarities between those two sources, we quantified the relationship, the statistic relationship, between the sources and used this relationship in order to produce a forecast of a more complete number of wounded persons, not only hospitalised but also non-hospitalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If I could follow up on that with just two questions. Number one, when you testified regarding deaths, you said that your effort was to actually count every single death that was violent and war related in the right area at the right time. You also made mention of another way that statisticians, demographers can do their work, and that is by taking a sample and then extrapolating from that sample to the population at large. Which approach did you follow when calculating numbers of wounded persons?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: So in the case of wounded persons, it wasn't a counting approach. We didn't have enough foundation for doing this. This is why we decided to go ahead with a small sample and one additional source that we used to produce statistical estimate, an extrapolation of certain relationship that we quantified between the two sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: My second question is: What kind of hospital records, I know they were from three hospitals and they were admissions and so forth, but people are admitted to the hospital for all sorts of reasons. What a records were put into the sample and what records were excluded from the sample?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, these were by all means only selected records. The selection was made by including only those patients admitted to hospitals that were either woman of any age, or men below age of 18 or above age 60. So men between 18 and 60 were excluded from our selection. So the sample can be seen as representing exclusively civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And what about the cause for which the person was admitted to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, as I mentioned earlier today, the cause is available as shelling or sniping. These are the two major causes of wounding. A third cause are cases where either shelling or sniping is mentioned jointly; for some reason, it was not possible to distinguish whether it was sniping or shelling. So there is a group of wounded persons who have a cause of wounding reported as sniping or shelling, and that is a very small margin of number of other causes which are not specified in terms of shelling or sniping, just other, in a very, very small number of these cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And what did you do with that very, very small number of cases that were other cases?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, we still kept in our database because all these persons were wounded persons and that was also reported in the hospital files. This is the reason why.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And at the end of putting together this sample and then extrapolating from this sampling, were you able to calculate minimum numbers of wounded persons in Sarajevo between August of 1994 and November of 1995?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. We have done such extrapolation and we calculated and estimated a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I want to refer now to Table 22 on page 54 and Table 25 on page 65 of the English version of your report and that would be slide number 2. Now, here you've calculate observed absolute minimum numbers, and then in Table 25 estimated more complete minimum numbers of wounded civilians. I'm going to ask to you define these two terms. Could you tell us what you mean by an observed absolute minimum number?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Observed absolute minimum numbers are just the numbers produced based on the sample of the hospital records, of civilians selected according to their age and sex criterion. I call this number minimum number because, as I mentioned, the sample does not include many other records available from other hospitals, like war hospitals and emergency help stations. It is also likely that certain files were destroyed during the war or certain records were never taken by the authorities. This often happens in this kind of conflict situations. We cannot be sure that records selected from hospital archives for use in and other projects is a complete selection of all relevant records. Nevertheless, it's good enough to use this record to obtain minimum, absolute minimum numbers, and this is what is presented in Table 22. An absolute minimum number of civilians wounded by any cause, mainly, of course, sniping, shelling, and possibly other causes, is 405. Of this number, 405, at least 254 were wounded by shelling; 77 by sniping; and another 70 were wounded, either by sniping or by shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So to sum it up, Table 22 is the sample. These are individuals for whom there is a hospital record that you can examine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: After the number wounded by shelling, 254, we have in parenthesis 185 plus 69, can you just tell us what the significance of the numbers in parenthesis are please?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: 185 is the number of cases in which shelling was reported as cause of wounding explicitly, so there is the use of term "shelling." And there are 69 additional cases for which the term "shelling" has not been explicitly used. But from the description of the circumstances of incidents, it is clear that these are also cases of wounded by shelling. So we call these cases implicit shelling cases and still include them under the same category of wounded by shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In Table 25, you then say there is an estimated, more complete minimum number of wounded civilians. That's at the bottom half of the slide that is on our screen. Can you tell us, please, the derivation or the source of these numbers that are in Table 25.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: These numbers were obtained from our modeling and extrapolation procedure. The procedure made use of the information or records reported as wounded persons from May 1992 -- sorry, April 1992 to July 1994, which is a period proceeding the indictment period, but by comparing the two sources hospital records that report only hospitalised patients only and Sarajevo household records that report on both hospitalised and non-hospitalised patients. So by comparing these two sources, we established a statistical model that described the relationship between those two types of records. This model is a quantification of the similarities between the sources. And the quality of the model, statistically speaking, is extremely high. There is no doubt that the tool as such as any deficiency. So using this estimated relationship, we made a forecast or extrapolation, which is the particular type of forecast that we made, and estimated, based on the observed numbers of records in the hospital files, the more complete number of patients of two types; hospitalised and non-hospitalised. These are the resulting numbers. We estimated actually several models. One for all cases jointly and some other models; one for shelling, one for sniping, and one for the shelling/sniping category.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And those are the numbers that are set forth in Table 25 on page 65 of your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please pause between question and answer for the sake of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you both hear that. Dr. Tabeau, please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Changing topics yet again, Dr. Tabeau. In your statistical analysis, were you able to draw any statistically based conclusions about whether civilians were deliberately targeted in Sarajevo between August of 1994 and November of 1995?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: We studied the relationship between killed civilians and killed military, in great detail. Based on this studies - we have conducted actually several types of studies of this relationship - I think there are good reasons to believe that there was targeting of civilian population in this particular conflict period in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If I could ask for slide number 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We're rushing and in a rush because this is the end of the procedure. So in my view, these questions should not be for the expert but the Chamber. I think that to save time, we ought to look at the expert part of her testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand. Are you saying she's not competent to give this evidence? Because I thought the next question now would be for her to explain how she would arrive at that kind of conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, the question that was asked was have the civilians - well, the civilians between quotation marks - have they been deliberately targeted. In my view, this is question which should not asked in the context of this expert testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, the Defence is saying this is a question which is properly for the Chamber. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Two things. First of all, what were the -- I have asked one question on this topic; and so if the objection is to foundation, I think I've got to attempt to lay the foundation and then Ms. Isailovic can challenge it -- point out where she feel it is lacking. If the question is -- if is the objection is that is one for the Chamber, what -- the ultimate question, of course, is for the Chamber. But what I have asked - and I was I think very careful with the way I phrase the question - is: As a statistician, can you draw statistical conclusions, not legal conclusions, statistical conclusions. I think that that is appropriate -- an appropriate question to put to this witness. And, thirdly, this is material that is in Dr. Tabeau' report. There is a mechanism by which the Defence can say that they challenge the qualifications of the expert to give all or any part of the report, and that was not done in this ways; rather, a request was made, and it will -- it's being followed today, that Dr. Tabeau be produced for cross-examination. That has been done. I also take the observation in that regard to be untimely. So given the carefully phrased manner of the question and given the timing of the objection, I would ask the Chamber to deny this submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, I think his best answer of the three is that these she's being asked to give a statistical conclusion not a legal conclusion. What do you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if the question is asked whether deliberately shooting civilians is a statistical matter, well, in my view, this is not the right question. In my cross-examination, I try to put all these data in perspective. In my view, these are precisely legal questions which should not be asked to the witness and not to experts. Anyway, you have already made a ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have not made a ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber's analysis is that if the witness, as a statistician, has some statistical method that can assist the Chamber in determining whether civilians were deliberately targeted, that's a matter on which she can testify. We will hear the method and then it is for us to maybe of it what we will. We may discard that piece of her evidence entirely, but let us hear what the method is. And I would be interested to find out, Mr. Docherty, whether this kind of evidence has been given in other cases. Are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I will ask the witness, but I can tell that you the answer will be that the data has never before been good enough to allow this to be done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear from the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The method concentrates on studying the ratios of killed civilians versus killed soldiers. These ratios are not knew in these kind of studies. I'm sure that in several other cases, these ratios were studied and presented. I think in this particular case, there is a very good foundation to look at the ratios very carefully and study them in several ways, and this is what we did. This kind of study I think is the first one that I present. So from this point of view, it is the first time that the ratios of civilians to soldiers were studied by month of the siege, by day of the siege, by the siege episode, and by both day and siege episode. And in addition to this, we also studied a selection of major dates from all six municipalities. So the extent that we have done this is for the first time so broad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm keen to hear the explanation, but I regret that I may not be here for the last session because I'm feeling indisposed, and so my colleagues will hear the explanation when we resume at the end of the break. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you have noticed, the President is absent; and under Rule 15 bis, the Chamber has decided to remain in session and I would like to give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, before the break, we were talking about statistical light that can be shed on the question of whether civilians were targeted. I'd like to continue with that now. We've talked so far today about numbers of killed and wounded civilians. Did you also track at least raw numbers of killed and wounded soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. We also produced statistics on soldiers killed in the siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And were you able to plot the killed and wounded soldiers on a time-line, if you will; in other words, develop a time pattern of when soldiers were killed and wounded?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: One correction regarding wounded person, we only studied the civilians. Regarding killed persons, these were both civilians and soldiers. So in this part of the testimony, I will be talking about the killed persons; civilians and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: So the question was about a time pattern of killings of soldiers and civilians. We did study these in several ways, most generally by looking at the numbers of killed civilians and soldiers by month, starting in August 1994 until November 1995. I have a figure in the report, figure -- figure 11, which illustrates these issues, and perhaps we can take a look at this figure right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And this figure is being broadcast, and if I could ask Mr. Usher to help you get had an in front of you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I think I have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just start with some basics. This is Figure 11 from your report, and it is found on page 39 of the English version. We have a number of different colours on this report, and we'll just go through them one after another from top to bottom -- actually not from top to bottom. The green colour represents what?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Represents soldiers. These are killed soldiers, records of killed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And the red area represents what?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: These are records of killed civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then there's a small grey area at the very top. What does that gray area mean?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is records of persons of whom we don't know, whether they were soldiers or civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Then along the horizontal axis, what is plotted?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is the time-line, say, starting months, basically speaking. These are the units that we used for this chart, starting with August 1994 until November 1995. It's the last month presented in this chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, on the left-hand side, along the vertical axis, what is being plotted?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is the axis that is used to show the scale for numbers of the deaths of killed, both civilians and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And then, lastly, there are a number of purple bars; and also on the right hand vertical axis, there's a different quantity being plotted. What is the significance of these purple bars and of the quantity on the right hand vertical axis?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The bars illustrate the ratios of killed civilians in relation to killed soldiers. The interpretation of this ratios is basically the number of the civilians killed per one killed soldier. These ratios are shown here in Figure 11, month by month. These are monthly data, and the level -- the values shown in the bars can be found in Figure 11 in the right-hand side axis. This is a different scale than the one on the left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, I want to start at a fairly general level and then come down to this specific case that we're in court about today. Is it possible for a statistician to determine, using statistical methods, whether two sets of data, whatever those data sets might be, whether two sets of data are varying with the same pattern or with a different pattern? Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Of course, in several ways. One of the ways is just making this kind of charts, as the one we have in front of us, just by showing the different series together in one chart. This is a cumulative presentation here, so the numbers of killed civilians go first; and on the top of them we show the numbers of killed soldiers, and on the top of them the numbers of individuals of unknown status. So the upper most line represents the overall time pattern, overall time pattern of killings of both civilians and soldiers and individuals of unknown status during the siege of Sarajevo starting in August 1994 until November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, purple bars that show the ratio between killed civilians verse killed soldiers, what does the size of this purple bar, the magnitude of the purple bar tell us about whether these two sets of data, killed civilians and killed soldiers, are varying the same way or a different way?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, this is what I wanted to add next, that the bars, that means the ration killed civilians to killed soldiers, is a way of expressing the structure of the data shown here in Figure 11. As we see there is no way that we can see the numbers of killed civilians proportionate and stable in the entire period, August 1994 to November 1995. So in certain periods, the ratios are higher; in certain other periods, the ratios are lower, telling us that the structure of the data, the proportion between of killed civilians versus killed soldiers is different; sometimes higher and sometimes lower.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, in your report, you divide days of the siege into what you call high days and what you call low days. Do you know what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. But before answering this question, I would like to make one more comment relating to Figure 11. It is important to notice that in Figure 11, there are in fact a few distinguished episodes shown as a general time pattern of killings. Obviously, there is one very high peek in the figure, the one associated with June 1995. But generally speaking already from March 1995 to August 1995, we can seek of a period of increased numbers of killed individuals. And there is an another period of increased numbers of killed individuals, starting in August 1994 until approximately December 1994. And there are two quieter episodes as well. The first quiet episode is in January/February 1995, and the second quieter episode is from September 1995 to November 1995. That's very important because later I will refer to this episodes. The two episodes with increased numbers of killed persons, will call high episodes, and the two other episodes with lower numbers of killed persons I will call low episodes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, the question was whether you had divided siege days into high days and low days. Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What is a high day?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: So addition to distinguishing high and low episodes, we also looked at the days, so the daily pattern of killings, and then we distinguished two types of day. Low days are days with less than three deaths per day, and high days with three or more deaths per day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Civilian --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is both. This was threshold that was used for the overall number, and it is only a threshold that is used to distinguish between days, not to calculate statistics: Low day versus high days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Why did you make that distinction? Why was it important to divide the siege into high and low days?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, the reason is that already in Figure 11, we saw something that was kind of an annoying result, meaning that the ratios, C to S ratio - I will call them civilians to soldiers, C to S, ratios - were obviously relatively high in quiet episodes, as opposed to low ratios in high episodes. So if we focus for a moment on the second high episode, the one with the highest number of killed persons in June 1995, that is the highest peak in Figure 11, if we look at it, and then if we look at the ratio, C to S ratios shown also in this figure, the lowest ratio, C/S ratio is obtained for the June 1995 for the month in which there is the highest number of killed persons. So, basically speaking, when the siege was becoming very active, the ratios, civilians to militaries, were dropping at the same time. This was some kind of annoying result, and we wanted to the study and to understand it better, because if we would find a confirmation of the picture in Figure 11, also with other data, daily data, for instance, then approximate it would tell us that even though siege was quiet in certain period, civilians were still killed, and in relative terms in higher numbers than in the very active siege periods. So this is why we decided to study low and high days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When you looked -- now, you have talked about the pattern that you see in Figure 11, which is deaths overall go up, ratio goes down; deaths overall go down, ratio goes up. When you divided into low and high day, what kind of a pattern did you see between the overall number of deaths and the ratio of killed civilians to killed soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: There is a table in the report, Table 18, in which ratios, C to S ratios, are shown for the low days and for the high days. I think it is a good idea to take a look at this table. So for the low days, the days in which less than three deaths were observed, the ratio is 1.6 civilian per one soldier. And for the high days, the days when three or more deaths were observed, the ratio is 0.9 civilians per one soldier. So this is just a beginning, yet another confirmation that what we saw in Figure 11 for the months and episodes of the siege is further seen in the daily data. So in order to present an even more complete picture, we studied both the low and high days, and the low and high episodes together. And we made a table in which these ratios are shown from this perspective, and this is Table -- as far as I remember, Table 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: On page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But we can also use the slide with -- with some major results from this table, and this is slide 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If we could see an excerpt from Table 20, it's slide number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, here, Dr. Tabeau, this is a portion of Table 20. It's on page 46 of the English version of the report, and here we see the division into phases that you talked about a minute ago when we were looking at Figure 11. Overall, what pattern do you see between killed civilians and killed soldiers based on this document that is on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, if we look -- well, perhaps I will explain table a little bit. As you said, it is an excerpt from Table 20. The absolute numbers of civilians and soldiers are skipped, and what is presented in slide 10 is only the values of the ratios, C to S ratios, which is the crucial part of this table. These ratios are shown, first of all, by the phases or episodes of the siege. As I said, there are two high phases, and there are two low phases. So the high phase is, first of all, August to December 1994. This is the first high episode, and the second high is from March to August 1995. And then we see in the same table in slide 10, low phases: The first one, January/February 1995; and the second one, September/November 1995. So the ratios for the episodes are shown in the last column in this table, which is called "all days," last column. And we see a very consistent result compared with Figure 11 discussed a few minutes ago, and with this little table that was number 18, which was already discussed. For high episodes, the ratios for high episodes are close to 1. That means for the first high episode, there is 1.1 civilians killed per 12 soldier; and for the second high episode, there is exactly 1 civilian killed per 1 soldier. For the low episodes, for January/February 1995, which is the first low episode, the ratio is 3.5 killed civilians per 1 soldier. And for the second low episode, the ratio is 1.7 killed civilian for 1 soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: So obviously for the low episodes, the ratios are higher than for the high episodes. This is one remark, first observation, from the data in this table. Now, we can take a look at these ratios -- at the ratios shown for the high and low days. So for every episode there are two additional C to S rations presented here; for instance, for first high phase, which is August/December 1994, we have two additional ratios. One is equal to 1.5 and the other one is 0.9. The first one relates to low days; the second one to high days. But we see the ratio for the low days in this particular episode is again higher than the ratio for the high days. And this observation holds for every episode, for all of them. The ratios on the low days are higher than the ratios on the high days. So all in all, it is yet another confirmation of what I said earlier, that obviously in quieter period of the siege, civilians were killed more frequently in relation to soldiers than on the more active episodes of the siege. But the question remains now: What about these very intense periods of the siege? Can't we make the same analysis of the ratios for those as well, and of course we can. So this analysis is available from the report, based on data from Table 21. Table 21 in the report is on page 47 of the English version. This Table contains data, a selection of certain data, that were used in a correlation analysis of the numbers of killed civilians with the number of killed soldiers. What kind of selection is included in Table 21? It is only the high days, that means days with three or more persons killed, in municipality of the Sarajevo Six. So these are selected dates, municipality by municipality, only dates -- this is Table 21, not 20. We are speaking of Table 21 now. Yes. Well, I still don't see Table 21 on my screen. This is Table 20 repeated, which is not a correct thing. We should be looking at Table 21, next one. This is why I'm waiting now for the Table. That's right. This is Table 21. This Table contains a selection of dates - this is just one part of the tables. There is another one on the next page - selection of dates where the number of killed persons were three or more by municipality. Numbers of the killed persons are shown by the military status, so civilians and soldiers and unknown status. All these three categories are shown separately. So the observations on the killed civilians -- on the number of number of killed civilians and the number of killed soldiers were used in a correlation analysis. In this analysis, a correlation coefficient was obtained, was calculated, between the number of killed civilians and the number of killed soldiers using this data from Table 21. This is correlation coefficient is a measure within a relationship between these two variables; number of killed civilians and number of killed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, I need to interrupt at this point. You have been going on for quite sometime about the data, and I think that you have told us that the number of killed civilians is not varying the same way as the killed soldiers and that in fact they are varying in different directions.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. If civilians were being killed as a by-product of military activity; that is to say, tragic but unintended consequences of intense fighting, then at the times in Figure 11, when the number of overall deaths goes, up would you expect the number of civilian deaths to go up proportionally or disproportionally?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I would expect it to go up proportionally, of course. That is the natural expectation one would have [indiscernible] casualties. This how it is usually, although it might differ depending on the military objectives of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And is that in fact the pattern that you are seeing; more intense activity, proportionally more civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is not; it is not. It an inverse relationship in statistical terms. So the increase in one number causes a decline in the other number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And from that inverse pattern, plus all the other data that we have been talking about for the past few minutes, are you able as a statistician to say whether this data sheds any light on question of whether civilians were being deliberately targeted, rather than dying accidently as the tragic but unintended consequence of military activity?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I would. Statistically speaking, yes, that is the case. So the very natural question one is asking in such a situation is: Well, if we assume that the number of casualties is a proxy for the number of military activities, in an area, so if there is a lot of activities, the number of casualties should also be higher relatively speaking. But we saw very quiet periods in the siege, but still we saw civilian casualties on these days, or even months, not only days. So I was asking myself, and not only me, other physician my team, how is it possible if there were no military activities or if there were no major military activities that civilians were still dying and we know they were dying of military -- of violent, war-related causes. Moreover, we see this pattern here. Based on a very minimum sample of the data, this analysis has all been done based on the on the absolute minimum numbers. Not corrected. These are the absolute minimum numbers. This is the smallest numbers that were produced in this report. So it's pretty sure that there were more casualties. We don't know how many exactly, but it is 100 per cent sure that there were more casualties. . And we also know that the way we define the status variable, we overestimated the militaries in our definition, not the civilians. So what can be expected is that the pattern is even more dramatic in the quieter periods than what we showed here in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask to you take a look at one more slide, and that will be power point slide number 9.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Table 21, if I can just finish it, the correlation coefficient, or is there no time for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: How about if you tell us what a correlation coefficient is.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It a measure of association between two variables; in this case, number of civilians and number of soldiers. In case of a perfect correlation, perfect linear association, the correlation coefficient is equal to one; and if is zero, that means there is no relationship between two variables. So the correlation coefficient calculated for Table 21 is 0.2, which certainly belongs to lower values measuring the relationship. The relationship is very weak.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, did you want to pursue that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The relation thus, between the number of civilian deaths and the military deaths, is not very strong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is very weak. This what is what I'm saying. Yes. I'm saying this based on the high days analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I have a number of questions relating to your method, but I don't want to the Prosecutor so maybe I will hold back my questions until you are finished, or maybe we should pursue my questions relating to the method. At this moment, unless you want to press on to something else, I leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: It's entirely up to you, Your Honour. I have one more slide, the one on the screen, and then I will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's have your slide then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, on the screen, I have asked for Figure 12.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I have it. I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, this seems to -- well, does include a large period of time that precedes the indictment period, and so let's start with the obvious preliminary question. If you as a statistician are asked to analyse statistics from August of 1994 to November 1995, how did does it help you do your work to go back all the way to April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, it helps a lot because it gives a broader context to the statistics obtained for this particular case, and it helps to understand better what kind of numbers we have been dealing with here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And on Figure 12a, it looks like - correct me if I'm wrong - the same presentation as if Figure 11?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, on the left, pre-indictment period, it seems that the purple bars are lower than they are during the indictment period. Am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, this is very correct. They are lower and the level is more uniform compared with the period after August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And from the greater size and lower uniformity after August of 1994, what conclusions do you, as a statistician, draw on the question of deliberate targeting of civilians during the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, this is very clear here. When looking at Figure 12a, obviously civilians were killed more frequently in relation to militaries in that period after August 1994. Well, I think for me, as a statistician, I see it as the basis for the statement about the targeting of civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So the inference of targeting of civilians, is it stronger, weaker, the same in the indictment period versus before the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, it is obviously stronger, the targeting of civilians in the indictment period than before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Judge Harhoff, that is all the questions I have on this topic. Also, I have one document to tender, and then I will be finished my direct examination. We passed out an errata sheet, Mr. President, at the beginning, and it has now been given a 65 ter number and put into e-court. It is 03127A, and I would ask that be admitted into evidence in lieu of having the witness go through her report and verbally make corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vous allez l'admettrez. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P638, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I remind the Prosecutor that you have 18 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That concludes my direct examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, as I said, I'm not sure I fully understand the statistical methods that you have applied in order to reach the conclusion that civilians are the deliberate target of attacks. If you look at Figure number 11, it would seem to me -- and can you also in fact look at the picture which is on the screen right now, Figure 12a. In both cases, it seems to me that the number of civilians killed during the period is really relatively stable. It increases while there is increased military activity, and you can see in Figure number 11, the green peak, you have from the months of May 1995 till August 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse the interruption. Would it be all right if we switched on the screen to Figure 11. We have figure 12a on there now. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Absolutely. But if I, as a non-statistician, were to evaluate this, I would say, Well, it really looks as if there is a relatively stable number of civilian deaths which increases when there is increased military activity. And maybe during those periods, it is true that the number of soldiers relative to the number of killed civilians of course increases, because increased military activity would make soldiers more susceptible to attacks and therefore also to death. This is my problem. This would only make sense if could you compare it with statistical data from other wars, because seen in isolation this tells you nothing. You would have to have a basis for comparison; not only a basis of comparison for other wars in which civilians are killed, but also comparison in terms of -- in terms of military sieges during armed conflict. Let me put to you another interpretation, not that I -- and again, I underline that I have no statistical knowledge or understanding, really. But if I were to say that when there is a military siege of an urban area, then there is a very natural number of deaths occurring among civilians. That goes with the very fact that it is a siege of a civilian area, of a town, or city. And that does not necessarily reflect the intention of the person who is holding the siege to target civilians. One could say it is collateral damage that occurs whenever you have sieges of civilian areas, urban areas. So I'm just reluctant to accept without any further explanation your conclusion that here in this case, in this particular case, civilians were deliberately and specifically targeted. So I wonder if you could help me out on this problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. You address three issues. The first one was additional results from other conflicts or other siege episodes or sieges generally. I think I already presented such data for the first two years of the siege in Sarajevo. Even though it is still the same area, urban area, we saw a very different pattern for the first two years than for the second two years; and, unfortunately, I don't have more results of this kind. I could have made some additional analysis for other episodes of the conflict in Bosnia because I have the sources. But for now we have two results. One is the pattern we see for the indictment period, August 1994 to November 1995; and the second one is April 1992 to July 1994. And, as we see, it is in Figure 12a that these patterns are quite different. I don't think that the circumstances changed in the first two years; and in the second two years of the siege, it was still the same Sarajevo, Sarajevo Six urban area. May I continue or --.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, yes. You may continue, but could I just kick in one observation. What Figure 12a shows us is that there were more military activity in the first half of the entire period.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. But still the pattern is relatively stable. If you look at the bars, it is. So that means that the proportion between civilian deaths and military deaths remained more or less stable in the first two years. So that means if we would redo this chart, and if we, one, show the cumulative pattern, I mean the areas, now they are shown on one on the top of the next, but if we could just make a line chart, which I did, then you would see the lines for civilians and military is more or less parallel. It is not the case for the next two years of the siege. The lines would cross, especially in the quieter periods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But would that not be a natural and logical result of the decrease in military activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But why would then civilians be killed if there was no military actions. That is my problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: There was still an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If you look at Figure 11, which shows the only the indictment period, then it is pretty obvious that civilian -- civilian deaths can be seen in the entire period. From the very beginning to the end, of course, they increased in the high episodes of the siege, meaning that there should be some deaths that could not be voided, and that means collateral damage. But, generally speaking, I personally have a problem when I know that siege was, say, kind of resting, there were no major war activities going on, but still civilians were killed; and if it comes to causes of wounding, because I have causes of wounding expressed as sniping/shelling, not for killed but I do have causes for the wounded persons, then you see from the causes that these were mainly victims of sniping in the quieter periods. That means people were shot. Why? If you refer to chart -- Figure 23, please, page 57. 23, page 37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This figure shows causes of wounding based on the sample of hospital records of Sarajevo. This is a clear figure, a clear chart. The red line is wounding by sniping; the blue one is wounding by shelling; and the last line, which is I think green or something like that, the dot-like line, is sniping and shelling jointly. So, actually, in the quieter periods, especially February, January/February, but also in the first active period or high period of the siege, that is from August to December 1994, there were quite some wounding caused by sniping. Sniping is there all the time, right? And in addition to sniping victims, we see wounded persons by shelling obviously, mostly in the second high episode, around June 1995, right? So that tells me shelling means major military activities going on, and obviously there were military activities going on, especially in the second high period, which was not the case really earlier, before this episode. But still people were shot by sniper obviously. So that is my reasoning. Well, if you look at these causes and the data, the time pattern in killings that we identified, based on completely different sources, and if we compare these two patterns, time pattern for wounded, time pattern for killed persons, if we calculate the correlation coefficient, the correlation is 0.99, which is almost 1. It is a perfect relationship between two. This tells me that I may think for the killed also about the same causes of the death as for the wounded, because the consistency of these two sources is incredible. It's almost an 1 to 1 correlation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Your figures may appear convincing, yet I am still uncertain as to the conclusions to be drawn from your figures, because I have no basis on which I can compare these figures. If we had before us information from previous military sieges of urban areas, which could provide us with some basis for comparison, I think I would feel more secure. But I'm simply not certain about how to -- how to interpret the information that you are putting to us. I have no idea of what sieges normally imply; but it may well turn out that when you have a military siege of an urban area, then there is inevitably a much higher degree of civilian casualties that you would normally expect in a war; and that then when in addition to the siege, there is then increased military activity, then the figure goes up more for soldiers than it does for civilians; and then finally as long as the siege goes on, and as long as during that siege there is an armed conflict, then civilian casualties are perhaps a, what do I call it, a collateral thing. I have no idea. I accept your figures and they look very convincing. I just don't now how to interpret them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may comment. Having this experience of so many years of working in the area of conflict statistics, I must admit there are no war episodes which are the same. I don't think there will be another siege, or in Bosnia, there was siege of Mostar. I don't think these two can be compared because all of them is just a unique case of a different situation. This is a very different situation from official statistics and western countries demography, where you can find a lot of similar results; of course, not of this type, but in that other area, that can be compared, that can be studied, and conclusions can be drawn. Conflict analysis is unique. There is nothing like a general picture of a conflict and conflict casualties. All I can say is that I think that we could look, me personally, into the statistics I made for the report, Mostar report, and think about whether or not there is anything similar in these two. But I still believe that the siege of Sarajevo should be seen as a unique case study. This is how it is, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I accept that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much, Witness. I'm now going to give the floor to Defence counsel for-- its cross-examination. You have 12 minutes, I believe, before we adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Branislav Isailovic. I am a member of the Paris Bar Association, and I am one of the lawyers representing Mr. Dragomir Milosevic. I shall give you my point of view which is point of view of a lawyer, not particularly well versed in mathematics, and I would like to address one sole point of your report. I don't have much time so I would like to start off with fairly basic items. Could you confirm that your executive summary is in fact the conclusion of your report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This is at the beginning, and this indicates it's either the conclusions that you made at the end of your report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I will start off by the heading or the title of area report, which included the word "siege." On page 1 of your report, if you turn to the footnote, you provide an explanation thereof and you state that you will indicate what a siege means.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. There is a footnote on this page. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In light of the previous questions that were put to you, from what I understand, the term "siege" is not a word which was used randomly. The term already means something, when you are conducting this kind of survey, in light of your expertise.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, we didn't use it as a random term, because this is a term that was commonly used.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't use -- I said it wasn't chosen by chance; in other words, the meaning is contained in it already. When you use the word "siege" and you use it as a title in your report, this already presupposes a certain meaning?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, as I explained in the footnote, it is used here to describe the presence of an armed conflict in Sarajevo in that time and blockade as well. And that's all. I think I didn't attach any other meanings to this word.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: From what you said, this doesn't only have to do with the presence of an armed conflict but of blockade as well?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, this is what it says in the footnote. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So where do you draw this conclusion, the fact that there was a blockade. Where do you draw this from?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Where did I draw this conclusion? I think from the many readings I did about the siege of Sarajevo, and that there were difficulties with providing international aid to the population of Sarajevo, that there was a shortage of food, that there was a shortage of medicines. I have read several reports, among others, by Physicians Without Borders. I think this are my sources for the term "blockade."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Given that your expert's report was commissioned by the Prosecutor, it wasn't the Prosecutor that gave you the information or that determined the title. The Prosecutor did not suggest the title, did it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No, they didn't. It was the title we proposed for the report. And, well, this is not my first report relating to Sarajevo, so I think I have some expertise in this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The siege which you review in your report, how important is it when you draw your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I understand the question, that you mean that the presence of an armed conflict, how important it was for -- to the conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: No. Let me spell this out a little bit. Sometimes difficult to understand each other when we don't speak the same language. Now, in your title, you use the expression "siege of Sarajevo." This is what you indicate in the title of your report. So this does have an impact on the conclusion you are to draw at the end of your expert report. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I don't think that the title can have any impact on the conclusions. The conclusions are the results from this research project and from the analysis of our sources. And, well, when proposing the title, we hoped to be clear and specific about what is this report about. And, as I'm saying, the siege is the presence of an armed conflict in the Sarajevo area in this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. I would like to pick up on this answer of yours. Your research project could have be entitled the dead and the wounded during the conflict that unfolded in Sarajevo area. Could that have been a title for your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, as I have very little time left, I would like to address the sources you have used. And in your report, right at the beginning of your report, from what I understood, there are two conflicts statistics and official statistics. In other words, you made the difference between the two, to begin with. Could you explain to us what difference there is between these two statistical methods.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I think this is a very good question, and official statistics usually are based on well established and complete sources. If not complete sources, then they are based on samples of which we know how large and how representative they are. So official statistics is a very different area from what we are able to present for -- in the conflict statistics. Even in countries like Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is absolutely exceptional source-wise, compared with other conflicts, I mean there are many sources, some relatively reliable and relatively complete, others less reliable, less complete, and some are really very bad as well, but source-wise Bosnia is very exceptional. Having said that, I still must admit it is not possible to produce complete statistics based on high quality complete sources. And this is the difference. We have to look at this report and at the statistics, keeping this in mind. The numbers are incomplete for many reasons, and of samples we often don't know how representative they are. But, still, we can use these samples, like the hospital records, knowing by comparison that the patterns obtained from this sample, samples, are very consistent with other results based on better sources. We can still go ahead with these kind of less complete sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Isailovic. It is now quarter to 2.00. We shall now adjourn and resume at tomorrow at 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, because we addressed this issue in the presence of Judge Robinson, what about motion 98 bis? I don't think we are going to wrap this up to tomorrow. I was able to get a reply from my colleague. Does this mean we shall address this issue, on Thursday morning, i.e., the 98 motion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we shall proceed the way we intended and hear the last witness, and then we will have the break, and we will start at 8.00 tomorrow morning, and then have the 98 bis motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is important. I need to pass on the information to Mr. Tapuskovic. I shall be questioning the witness. So we will start tomorrow; is that right? Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 2nd day of May, 2007, at 8.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
